deep.reconstruction:
This is the title page and opening of E260 (Novi Commentarii Academiae Scientiarum Petropolitanae 6, for 1756/57, printed 1761). There is no mathematics yet; it states the problem the memoir serves.

§1 states an empirical fact. Water driven through channels or pipes loses a considerable part of its motion, and the loss grows with pipe length and with narrowness. The clearest case is the fountain jet. Ideal hydrodynamics (Bernoulli's principle for steady inviscid flow, the Torricelli relation v^2 = 2gh) predicts that water piped from a reservoir should rise nearly to the reservoir's height. In fact the jet never reaches that height, and it falls further short the longer and narrower the pipes. In modern terms this is head loss, which the Darcy–Weisbach form writes as h_f = f (L/D) v^2/(2g). The loss increases with L/D, which matches Euler's qualitative description.

§2 makes a methodological claim. Practitioners distrust the theory because of this discrepancy. Euler argues that the theory rests on the most certain principles of mechanics, so its truth is not weakened. Instead one must look for physical circumstances that the theory left out.

The next page names the cause as friction or rubbing (attritus) of the water against the pipe walls, by analogy with the friction of solids. Euler claims that no earlier author had determined, or even tried to investigate, the laws of this friction. The memoir then goes on to model the fluid as made of small solid particles with Amontons-type friction at the wall.
errors: None on this page. The qualitative empirical claims are correct: head loss grows with L/D. Euler's later modelling choice of Amontons-type friction proportional to pressure is not the right law for fluids, but that choice appears on later pages, not here.

ideas.what: Discrepancy between ideal-fluid prediction (fountain rising to reservoir height) and experiment, attributed to resistance growing with pipe length and narrowness
ideas.modern_name: Frictional head loss in pipe flow (Darcy–Weisbach / Hagen–Poiseuille scaling with L/D)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Qualitatively Mariotte, Couplet, Bossut and others in the 17th–18th c.; quantitatively Chézy (1770s), Prony, Hagen (1839), Poiseuille (1840), Darcy (1857), Weisbach (1845)
ideas.where_published: E260 itself; discussed by Truesdell in his Opera omnia Series II introduction on fluid mechanics (Rational Fluid Mechanics 1687–1765)

ideas.what: Methodological defence of theory: disagreement with experiment points to omitted physical effects, not to false principles
ideas.usually_credited_to: General scientific methodology; Euler voices it repeatedly
ideas.where_published: E260; similar remarks in Euler's hydraulic papers of the 1750s

deep.surprise_reason: This is an introductory page stating the well-known motivating problem of a published and catalogued memoir. Truesdell and others have discussed E260's friction model, and there is no new mathematics here.
transcription_corrections: '(o)' in the header is a decorative printer's ornament, not text.
Otherwise the transcription matches the image (long-s forms such as 'teſtatur', 'ſalientibus', 'aſſurgere', 'deſcenderat' are faithful).
